## 1. From text to numbers

Computers are good at numbers, but text is just strings. Before we can
analyse text, we need to translate it into numbers. The workhorse is the
**document-feature matrix (dfm)**: one row per document, one column per
word, and each cell counts how many times a word appears in a document.

R has a dedicated package for text analysis: **quanteda**. It also ships
a built-in corpus of 60 US presidential inaugural addresses, which we
will use for the whole tutorial.

```{r}
library(quanteda)

corp <- data_corpus_inaugural   # 60 speeches, 1789-2025

corp                            # what is inside?
docvars(corp)                   # Year, President, Party for each speech

# Step 1: split each speech into words (tokens), drop punctuation
tok <- tokens(corp, remove_punct = TRUE)

# Step 2: count words per document -> the document-feature matrix
dfm_t <- dfm(tok)

dfm_t                           # 60 documents x 9,573 word types
```

A dfm is a table: rows are speeches, columns are words. Nearly all of
today's methods start from this table.

## 2. Dictionary methods

The dictionary method counts how often words from a **predefined list**
appear in each document. The researcher decides what matters, and R does
the counting.

### A mini dictionary of our own

```{r}
mini <- dictionary(list(
  war     = c("war", "battle", "military", "soldiers"),
  peace   = c("peace", "harmony", "friendship"),
  economy = c("economy", "tax", "trade", "industry")
))

counts <- dfm_lookup(dfm_t, mini)  # count list words in each speech
counts                             # 60 docs x 3 categories

head(convert(counts, to = "data.frame"))
```

`dictionary()` takes a list of word lists. `dfm_lookup()` counts the
matches. This is how classic content analysis works - transparent and
reproducible, because anyone can read the word list.

### A real dictionary: Lexicoder Sentiment (LSD)

The Lexicoder Sentiment Dictionary (Young & Soroka 2012) contains lists
of positive words ("happy", "freedom", "progress") and negative words
("war", "crisis", "fear"). It ships with quanteda:

```{r}
data_dictionary_LSD2015            # have a look at the lists

pos_neg <- dictionary(list(
  positive = data_dictionary_LSD2015$positive,
  negative = data_dictionary_LSD2015$negative
))

sent <- dfm_lookup(dfm_t, pos_neg)    # 60 x 2 counts

# a sentiment score for each speech: (pos - neg) / (pos + neg)
tab <- cbind(docvars(corp), convert(sent, to = "data.frame"))
tab$score <- with(tab, (positive - negative) / (positive + negative))

head(tab[, c("Year", "President", "Party", "score")], 10)
```

The score runs from -1 (all negative words) to +1 (all positive words).

```{r}
# Sentiment over time, coloured by party
plot(tab$Year, tab$score,
     pch = 19,
     col = as.numeric(factor(tab$Party)),
     xlab = "Year", ylab = "sentiment score")

# average sentiment by party
tapply(tab$score, tab$Party, mean)
```

Which president was most positive? most negative? Any pattern?

> A dictionary measures the *presence* of topics. It cannot tell you
> *how* the topic is discussed ("not happy" is not "happy"). Keep that
> in mind.

## 3. Topic modelling

A dictionary needs you to decide the categories in advance. **Topic
modelling** turns it around: the algorithm discovers themes from the
data. Words that often travel together ("goal", "match", "coach") signal
a latent topic. LDA (Latent Dirichlet Allocation, Blei et al. 2003) is
the classic algorithm:

- each document is a **mixture** of topics
- each topic is a **distribution** over words

### Fit an LDA model

```{r}
library(topicmodels)

# clean the dfm: remove stopwords ("the", "of" ...) and very rare words
dfm_clean <- dfm(tokens_remove(tok, stopwords("en")))
dfm_clean <- dfm_trim(dfm_clean, min_docfreq = 5)

# convert the dfm to the format topicmodels expects
dtm <- convert(dfm_clean, to = "topicmodels")

set.seed(2026)                     # LDA is random - fix the seed!
lda <- LDA(dtm, k = 5, control = list(seed = 2026))
```

`k` is the number of topics to look for - your choice.

```{r}
terms(lda, 8)          # top 8 words of each topic
```

The model only gives word lists. **You** name the topics. Can you give
each of the 5 topics a label?

```{r}
topics(lda)                        # most likely topic for each speech
tail(topics(lda), 6)               # the last six presidents

posterior(lda)$topics              # 60 x 5: share of each topic per speech
posterior(lda)$topics["2017-Trump", ]   # topic shares of one speech

# how much of the corpus is each topic?
colMeans(posterior(lda)$topics)
```

```{r}
# Which topics dominate? Try a simple barplot
share <- posterior(lda)$topics
barplot(colMeans(share), names.arg = 1:5,
        xlab = "topic", ylab = "average share")
```

Try k = 4 and k = 6. Which k gives topics you can actually name?

> Topic models *propose* structure. Garbage in, garbage out - and even
> good output needs a human to interpret it.

## 4. Embeddings

Counting treats "war" and "battle" as completely different columns - but
they mean similar things. **Word embeddings** fix this: every word
becomes a dense vector of numbers (here: 50 numbers), trained on the
idea that similar words appear in similar contexts (Firth 1957). Similar
meanings end up close together in vector space.

We use **GloVe** vectors (Pennington et al. 2014) trained on 6 billion
tokens of Wikipedia and news. A compact version of the top 30,000 words
is saved in this folder so everything works offline:

```{r}
glove <- readRDS("glove_top30k.rds")   # 29999 words x 50 numbers
dim(glove)

glove["democracy", ]                   # one row = one word vector
```

### Similarity

The distance between two word vectors is their **cosine similarity**: 1
= same direction, 0 = unrelated, -1 = opposite.

```{r}
cos_sim <- function(a, b) sum(a * b) / sqrt(sum(a^2) * sum(b^2))

cos_sim(glove["war", ], glove["peace", ])          # 0.644
cos_sim(glove["war", ], glove["battlefield", ])    # 0.636
cos_sim(glove["war", ], glove["banana", ])         # ?
```

### Nearest neighbours

```{r}
nearest <- function(word, n = 8) {
  sims <- apply(glove, 1, function(r) cos_sim(glove[word, ], r))
  sort(sims, decreasing = TRUE)[2:(n + 1)]   # skip the word itself
}

nearest("democracy")
nearest("immigration")
nearest("inequality")
```

The neighbours are not synonyms from a dictionary - the model learned
them from 6 billion tokens of real text. Try your own words: "gender",
"protest", "internet".

### The analogy trick

```{r}
# king - man + woman = ?
target <- glove["king", ] - glove["man", ] + glove["woman", ]
sort(apply(glove, 1, function(r) cos_sim(target, r)),
     decreasing = TRUE)[1:6]
```

Try `paris - france + china`. What do you get?

### Visualising word vectors

```{r}
words <- c("democracy","freedom","war","peace","economy","tax",
           "family","education","science","internet","immigration",
           "inequality","government","rights","market","religion")

pca <- prcomp(glove[words, ], scale. = TRUE)  # shrink 50-d to 2-d

plot(pca$x[, 1], pca$x[, 2], type = "n",
     xlab = "PC1", ylab = "PC2")
text(pca$x[, 1], pca$x[, 2], labels = words, cex = 0.9)
```

Words that cluster together are used in similar contexts. Which clusters
do you see?

> Important: embeddings are mirrors of their training corpus - they
> inherit its biases (Bolukbasi et al. 2016). Treat them as data about
> society, not neutral facts.

## 5. LLMs

Dictionaries, topic models and embeddings all reduce text to numbers.
**Large language models** (GPT, Claude, DeepSeek, Llama...) take a
different route: they read the text and follow an instruction. They can
classify, extract or summarise text with zero (or a few) examples, which
makes them powerful *annotators* for research.

The workflow is: design the task -\> write the prompt -\> call the API
-\> **validate a sample yourself**.

In R, the package is **ellmer**:

```{r llm, eval=FALSE}
library(ellmer)

# Option 1: a cloud API (works with DeepSeek, ChatGPT, any OpenAI-compatible API)
chat <- chat_openai(
  system_prompt = "You are a sociology research assistant. Classify each news headline into ONE topic: Economy, Politics, Culture, or Technology. Reply with only the topic name.",
  base_url = "https://api.deepseek.com",       # DeepSeek; ChatGPT uses the default
  api_key = Sys.getenv("DEEPSEEK_API_KEY")     # never put the key in your script!
)


```

`Sys.getenv("DEEPSEEK_API_KEY")` reads the key from your environment, so
the key never appears in the script itself. You can set it in R with
`Sys.setenv(DEEPSEEK_API_KEY = "your-key")` for the current session.

If you have no API access, read the example file in this folder - it
contains five headlines classified by a local deepseek-r1 model:

```{r}
ex <- jsonlite::fromJSON("llm_example.json")
ex
```

Do you agree with all five labels?

> Model answers are proposals to verify, not facts. Always check a
> sample yourself, and report the model, version and prompt you used.

## 6. Hands-on: four methods on one corpus

One corpus - the 60 inaugural speeches - four methods.

### A. Dictionary

```{r}
# 1. design your own mini dictionary (e.g. freedom / slavery / religion)
# 2. count it in the speeches with dfm_lookup()
# 3. which president uses your words most?
```

### B. Topic model

```{r}
# 1. fit LDA with k = 4 and k = 6 (set.seed(2026))
# 2. label the topics from their top words
# 3. posterior(lda)$topics["2021-Biden", ] - which topic dominates?
```

### C. Embeddings

```{r}
# 1. nearest("democracy") - already done above; try three words of your own
# 2. the analogy: paris - france + china
# 3. add two words of your choice to the PCA plot - do they land where you expect?
```

### D. LLM

```{r}
# 1. classify these three headlines yourself FIRST (human coder!)
# 2. then classify them with chat_openai() or chat_ollama()
# 3. compare: where do you and the model disagree?

headlines <- c(
  "Hong Kong announces measures to support first-time home buyers",
  "City orchestra wins international award for contemporary music",
  "Unemployment rate drops to a 10-year low"
)
```

### Reflection questions

- Which method would you use to (a) replicate a published coding scheme,
  (b) explore a brand-new corpus, (c) measure how similar two documents
      are, (d) code thousands of open-ended survey answers?
- What does each method miss?
